Learning Objectives
Review the mechanism of injury for superior labrum anterior to posterior lesions. 
List the subtypes of labral pathology and pathology associated with superior labrum anterior
to posterior lesions.
Describe the clinical examination to evaluate pathology in overhead athletes. 
Explain the appropriate treatment plan based on specific subtype and activity.
List the risk factors for ulnar collateral ligament injuries in overhead athletes. 
Describe a full-body clinical examination to determine the main cause of ulnar collateral
ligament injuries.
Review a criterion-based program with the goal of returning to overhead throwing.

Superior Labrum Anterior to Posterior Tears/Lesions
Pathoanatomy/Pathophysiology
Overview
Superior labrum anterior to posterior (SLAP) lesions are common.
Commonly observed in athletes, especially overhead athletes
Commonly result from traumatic injury
Often present with normal wear and tear on the shoulder in the general population

Overview
Superior labrum anterior to posterior lesions are common injuries that may vary in
presentation and mechanism of injury based on the patient population in which they
occur. Recently, management of these injuries in overhead athletes has changed,
shifting from a surgical to nonsurgical treatment approach because of poor outcomes in
players attempting to return to the same level of play. Initial stages of management
focus on pain reduction, restoration of motion, and scapular strengthening, whereas
later stages of management focus on muscular balance and dynamic stabilization to
prepare for overhead throwing.
Injury Classification
Ten subtypes of labral pathology exist based on associated instability and posterior
extension1,2 (Figure 1). Although a clinical examination can be performed to determine
pathology, MRI is extremely sensitive (96%) and may aid in identifying specific subtypes of a
lesion.
1. Degenerative mechanism characterized by fraying of the superior glenoid labrum with the
peripheral labrum and the biceps anchor firmly attached to the glenoid

8. Involves a type II tear with a posterior labrum extension to the 6-o’clock position
9. A circumferential lesion involving the full 360° of the labral attachment to the glenoid rim
10. Involves a superior labrum tear combined with a posteroinferior labrum tear (reverse
Bankart lesion)

Figure 1 Illustrations show the types of superior labrum anterior to posterior lesions, including
modifications. Type I includes superior labrum fraying and degeneration. Type II involves a
detached superior labrum and biceps anchor from the superior glenoid. Type III involves a
bucket-handle tear of the superior labrum but an intact biceps anchor. Type IV lesions include a
type III bucket-handle tear that extends into the biceps tendon root. Type V lesions include
anteroinferior Bankart disruption in continuity with a type II lesion. Type VI lesions include a type
II lesion with an unstable labral flap. Type VII lesions involve extension of a type II tear through
the capsule under the middle glenohumeral ligament. Type VIII lesions are a type II variant with
extensions into the posterior labrum. Type IX lesions are type II tears with circumferential labral
involvement. Type X tears are a type II lesion with posteroinferior labral disruption.
Most common SLAP lesions

through phases of the overhead throwing raise the labrum off the glenoid rim.6
Repetitive overhead throwing: specifically, the peel-back mechanism in baseball players,
in which abduction and external rotation cause a rotational force at the biceps tendon;

Concomitant pathology
45% of patients (73% of baseball pitchers) with a superior labral lesion also have a partial-
thickness tear of the supraspinatus portion of the rotator cuff.24
11% of patients with a SLAP lesion have a complete rotator cuff tear.
22% of patients with a SLAP lesion have a Bankart lesion of the anterior glenoid.16
Type I lesions typically are associated with rotator cuff pathology.
Type II lesions vary, with younger patients reporting clinical instability and older patients
often presenting with rotator cuff pathology.
Type III/type IV lesions often are associated with traumatic instability.25

Clinical Examination
A comprehensive subjective history including, the exact mechanism of injury, must be
obtained. In addition, the patient should clearly define all overhead activities and sports
participation. The clinician should remember that although labral pathology frequently
presents as repetitive overuse conditions, such as those observed in overhead athletics,
patients also may describe a single traumatic event, such as a fall onto an outstretched
arm, sudden traction, or a blow to the shoulder. Patients may present with nonspecific
complaints but typically report intermittent pain that increases with overhead activity.
Patients report pain with specific movements, such as mechanical symptoms of painful
clicking or catching of the shoulder. The most predictive subjective problem in overhead
athletes is the inability to perform sports activity at a high level. Synder et al8 reported
that 50% of overhead athletes describe a loss of velocity and accuracy associated with
uneasiness of the shoulder.
The physical examination should include a complete evaluation of bilateral
glenohumeral passive and active range of motion (ROM). The experience of the authors
of this lesson suggests that patients with a SLAP lesion often exhibit pain with passive
external rotation at 90° of shoulder abduction, especially with the application of
overpressure. In addition, a painful arc of motion may be present, particularly with active
arm elevation. Many potentially useful special tests/maneuvers have been described to
determine the presence of labral pathology in overhead throwers, including the active

supination and external rotation test, and pronated load test.
Labral injuries commonly occur in combination with pathology of other structures of the
shoulder complex. Younger individuals typically present with clinical instability, whereas
older patients present with rotator cuff pathology. Andrews et al24 reported that 45% of
patients with a superior labral lesion also have a partial-thickness tear of the
supraspinatus portion of the rotator cuff, which is discovered during arthroscopic
assessment; note that 73% of the patients in this group were baseball pitchers.

Type I SLAP Lesions (Nonsurgical Treatment Approach)
The rate of progression through rehabilitation is based on the presence and extent of
concomitant lesions. In patients with a type I lesion, the biceps labral anchor is stable
and intact, which allows for a progressive approach to restoration of motion and
function. The rehabilitation program is focused on decreasing pain, obtaining muscle
balance, and re-establishing dynamic humeral head control to promote stability of the
glenohumeral and scapulothoracic joints, which allows the athlete to return to overhead
throwing without symptom reproduction.
Type II SLAP Lesions (After Surgical Repair)
Phase I: immediate postoperative phase (day 1 to week 6)
Goals
Protect the anatomic repair.
Promote healing of repaired tissue.
Prevent negative effects of immobilization.
Promote dynamic stability.
Diminish pain and inflammation.
Address posture (scapular position).

Sleep in immobilizer for 4 weeks

Type II SLAP lesions are common in overhead athletes, usually involving biceps tendon
detachment from the glenoid rim with frequent observation of a peel-back lesion. In
designing a rehabilitation protocol, clinicians must determine the extent of the lesion
and the exact location and number of suture anchors used. Compared with a type I/III
lesion, postoperative progression is slower for type II lesions to allow for healing of the
more extensive anatomic repair that was necessary to reattach the biceps tendon
anchor. The initial concern during rehabilitation is to appropriately control forces and
loads on the repaired labrum while decreasing pain and restoring ROM. Patients will
progress to a strengthening program that promotes proprioception, dynamic stability,
neuromuscular control, and co-contraction of the entire shoulder musculature to
address the underlying glenohumeral joint instability that often is observed in patients
with a SLAP lesion. Lastly, patients progress through a plyometric and criterion-based
return-to-throwing program aimed at returning overhead athletes to their prior level of
play.
Ulnar Collateral Ligament Injuries
Pathoanatomy/Pathophysiology
Overview

Overview
Ulnar collateral ligament (UCL) injury is extremely common in overhead throwing
athletes because the ligament is the primary restraint to valgus stress in the elbow.
Recently, the rate of surgical procedures in baseball athletes has continued to rise at an
alarming rate. Although baseball pitching particularly is associated with a high incidence
of UCL pathology because of repetitive microtrauma involved in the stresses of overhead
throwing, UCL injury has been reported in patients who participate in other sports, such
as javelin; tennis; gymnastics; and collision sports, such as football and wrestling, and in
patients who fall onto an outstretched arm. Rettig et al29 reported that approximately
one-half of UCL injuries can be successfully managed nonsurgically, and patients are
able to return to the same level of activity. Surgical management should be considered
in patients in whom symptoms do not resolve or if the injury occurs in an acute,

traumatic fashion in high-velocity overhead throwers or individuals with increased laxity
who perform contact or weight-bearing activity. Reconstruction of the UCL was the
primary method of surgical fixation for many years; however, repair with internal fixation
recently became a treatment option. Both procedures, if paired with an appropriate
rehabilitation program, are associated with excellent outcomes with regard to returning
patients to their prior level of play.
Incidence of Injury
Most injuries with regard to overhead athletes result from cumulative valgus stress on the
medial elbow during repetitive activity. The risk of injury increases with higher-velocity,
increased repetitions and throwing in a fatigued state. UCL injuries primarily affect overhead
throwing athletes.
UCL injuries can occur in javelin throwers, gymnasts, and collision athletes.
Primary restraint to valgus stress in the elbow
Most injuries are secondary to cumulative valgus stress on the medial elbow during repetitive
overhead athletic activity.
Baseball pitchers exhibit the highest incidence of UCL injury and surgical reconstruction.30,31
UCL injuries have been reported in athletes who participate in other overhead sports,
including American football, tennis, and javelin throwing.32-34

serious elbow injury in youth baseball35

pitchers38,42

Epidemic rate of UCL injuries in Major League Baseball (MLB)43
Elbow injuries in MLB account for 16 to 22% of all injuries.44,45
Conte et al31 investigated injury rates in the minor leagues and in MLB and estimated that

has been performed in 25% of MLB pitchers.
Chalmers et al46 noted that higher pitch velocity is the most predictive factor for undergoing

Clinical Examination
Patient history
A thorough patient history and physical examination are crucial.
Treatment recommendations depend heavily on injury- and patient-specific characteristics.47
Athlete age, sport, position, level of participation, future aspirations, and willingness to
change sport or position should be considered.48
Symptom duration, previous episodes, and location of pain
Any recent change in velocity, accuracy, and endurance
85% of pitchers experience symptoms during the acceleration phase of throwing.49
A sudden onset with an associated pop or a gradual progression of pain with decreased
pitching speed and control
Overuse injury risk factors need to be determined.
Physical examination
Physical examination of the entire upper quarter, core, and hip/pelvis should be conducted.
Loss of hip internal rotation and/or total rotational motion is more frequently observed in
overhead throwers who experience an UCL injury compared with those who do not.50
Decreased lumbopelvic control during single-leg balance and step-up activities that mimic
control required during throwing also correlate with an increased incidence of elbow injury in
overhead athletes.51
Thorough evaluation of the shoulder joint should be performed in overhead athletes.
Loss of flexion and/or reduced total rotational motion was the most considerable correlation
to UCL injury in professional pitchers.52
Reduced total rotational motion and glenohumeral internal rotation deficit are risk factors
for UCL injury.53

Special tests

Valgus stress test

Preferred special test (Wilk): prone valgus stress tests (Figure 2)
Patient is placed in the prone position to stabilize the shoulder. The forearm is pronated
to pre-tension muscle tissue, and the elbow is flexed 20° to 30°, which further isolates the
medial aspect of the elbow and improves the ability for the clinician to directly assess the
anterior band of the UCL.

Clinical Examination
A thorough patient history is important to determine the factors that may affect the
course of treatment. The clinician should determine the patient’s playing history,
including number of teams, positions played, playing schedule, level of play, and future
aspirations to create a long-term plan. In addition, delineation of the onset of symptoms
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:59 PM
AAOS | Rehabilitation for Shoulder and Elbow Injuries in Overhead Athletes
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004083
18/36

is important because many patients experience arm pain for longer periods than the
time at which first reports are made. The clinician should determine the timing and the
manner in which the injury occurred (gradually over time versus a sudden pop with one
pitch). Clinicians also should determine if symptoms are reproduced with throwing
motion because this often will occur during the transition from the late-cocking phase to
the early-acceleration phase. The patient, caregiver, and coaches should be educated on
the proposed treatment plan to prevent overuse and decrease the risk of return to
sports activity too soon.
The clinician should perform a complete body examination that includes the upper
quarter as well as the core, hips, and pelvis because these structures may contribute to
UCL injuries. Increased attention should be exercised during evaluation of the shoulder
joint in overhead athletes because loss of flexion and/or total rotational motion are
substantially correlated with UCL injuries. Lumbopelvic stability and hip internal rotation
motion deficits are more prevalent in overhead throwers who experience an UCL injury
and, therefore, must be assessed. Palpation along the UCL and the flexor pronator mass
should be performed because tenderness may indicate underlying pathology. Lastly,
special tests can be performed to determine the location of injury. The moving valgus
stress test is the most specific and sensitive examination for UCL injuries. The milking
maneuver can be performed to determine posterior band involvement, whereas the
valgus stress test can be performed to isolate the anterior band and determine
pathology at this location.
Imaging Studies
Chronic UCL insufficiency may result in ossification along the UCL, which can be observed on
plain radiographs.
Conventional MRI can identify ligament thickening from chronic injury and large, full-thickness
tears.47
Magnetic resonance arthrography improves diagnostic sensitivity for partial-thickness
tears.57,58

UCL Reconstruction
In the initial phase after surgical reconstruction, postoperative rehabilitation will vary
based on the surgical approach and the condition of the flexor pronator origin.
Knowledge of the surgical approach is important to allow the rehabilitation clinician to
appropriately guide and progress the patient through ROM and resistive exercises.
Figure-of-8 involves complete detachment of the flexor/pronator origin from the medial
epicondyle; therefore, additional care must be exercised to not overstretch these
muscles via active wrist extension during the initial six postoperative weeks. The
modified Jobe procedure involves the use of a muscle-splitting approach that does not
interfere with the flexor/pronator origin, allowing for more aggressive early ROM of the
